title: About Us

description: How a former analytical chemist ended up roasting coffee — the story of Hearth & Bean and the people behind the counter.
body:
![Whole coffee beans scattered across a cream background](assets/images/beans.svg)

# About Hearth & Bean

I spent eight years in a lab before I spent a single day behind an espresso machine.

I'm Priya Sathe, and before Hearth & Bean I worked as an analytical chemist, mostly running HPLC and titration panels for a food-testing lab. It was careful, exacting work — measure twice, calibrate the instrument, don't trust a result you can't reproduce. I didn't expect any of it to be useful for making coffee. It turned out to be the most useful thing I know.

## How This Started

I got into coffee the way a lot of people in this industry did: badly, at home, with a bag of supermarket beans and a French press that made something bitter and thin no matter what I did. A friend gave me a bag of freshly roasted single-origin coffee and a scale for my birthday, mostly as a joke. I brewed it by weight instead of guessing, and it was such a different drink that I assumed I'd done something wrong. I hadn't. I'd just been measuring nothing, for years, and calling it coffee.

That set off the part of my brain that likes variables. Why does a finer grind extract faster? What is actually happening when coffee "blooms"? Why did the same beans taste different at two cafés three blocks apart? I started reading everything I could find — Illy's papers on extraction, the SCA water standard, roasting logs from small roasters willing to publish them — and within a year I had a home setup that would have embarrassed a small café: a refractometer, three brewers, a scale accurate to a tenth of a gram, and a spreadsheet I am not proud of.

## Why a Shop

I opened Hearth & Bean in 2019 because I wanted to roast coffee the way I used to run a lab panel: with real measurements, a repeatable process, and enough curiosity to keep asking why. Most of what makes coffee good or bad is invisible unless you go looking for it — extraction yield, total dissolved solids, water hardness, roast development time — and I wanted a place where we took that seriously without making the person waiting for their morning latte sit through a lecture. You can get a excellent, unremarkable cup here in ninety seconds. You can also ask a question that turns into a twenty-minute conversation. Both are the point.

We started as a two-person filter bar with a single sample roaster in the back corner. We now roast on a 12kg drum roaster three mornings a week, run six espresso-based drinks and a rotating filter list, and employ eleven people, several of whom know more about coffee than I do at this point and are better baristas besides.

## What We Believe In

**Traceability over marketing.** Every bag we sell lists the farm or cooperative, the varietal, the processing method, and the elevation, because that information changes how you should brew it and because the people who grew it deserve the credit.

**Freshness over convenience.** We roast in small batches and sell out of bags regularly rather than keeping a large buffer stock. Coffee is at its best 4–14 days after roasting; we would rather run out on a Tuesday than sell you something stale.

**Direct and long-term relationships.** We buy the large majority of our green coffee through direct trade relationships with importers who visit the farms every season, and we've bought from several of the same cooperatives for four years running. Continuity lets farmers plan, and it lets us actually taste how a lot changes year to year.

**Teaching, not gatekeeping.** Specialty coffee has a reputation for being precious about itself. We try hard not to be. If you want the science, we'll give you the science. If you just want a good flat white, we will never make you feel like you're doing coffee wrong.

## The Space

We're a narrow shop on Marlow Street with eighteen seats, a bar you can watch the espresso machine from, and a back corner where the roaster runs on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday mornings — if you're here early, you'll smell it before you see it. We're a genuinely good place to sit with a laptop, and an even better place to put the laptop away and talk to whoever's next to you.

Come say hello. Ask us what's on the filter bar today. We're glad you're here.

— Priya and the Hearth & Bean team

![A cup of coffee, steaming, on a warm amber background](assets/images/hero.svg)

# Welcome to Hearth & Bean

We roast in small batches, brew with more care than is strictly necessary, and are always happy to talk about water chemistry with anyone who asks — and several people who didn't.

Hearth & Bean is a coffee roastery and café on Marlow Street. We roast twice a week, pull espresso all day, and keep a rotating lineup of single-origin filter coffee for anyone who wants to taste a farm rather than a blend. If you want a straightforward oat flat white, we will make you a very good one. If you want to know why the Kenyan lot tastes like blackcurrant, we will happily keep you at the counter for twenty minutes explaining processing methods.

## What's Here

**[The Menu](menu.md)** — everything we pour, everything we bake, and what it costs.

**[The Nerdy Stuff](the-nerdy-stuff.md)** — extraction, water chemistry, roast curves, and the other things we think about more than is healthy.

**[The Journal](journal-index.md)** — single-origin release notes, brewing guides, and dispatches from the roastery.

**[Visit & Order](visit-and-order.md)** — hours, address, online ordering, subscriptions, and how to get a bag of beans to your door.

## From the Journal

```mdcms
posts-created-reversechronological
limit: 6
paginate: yes
```

## A Note on What We're Doing Here

We are not trying to reinvent coffee. Filter and espresso have been done well for a long time; our job is mostly to buy good green coffee, roast it competently, and not get in its way. Where we spend our energy is on the things that are easy to get wrong quietly — grind consistency, water quality, dose accuracy, freshness — because those are the variables that separate a fine cup from a forgettable one, and most of them are invisible unless someone tells you to look for them.

Come in, sit down, and ask us anything. We like the questions as much as the coffee.

description: The coffee science behind Hearth & Bean — extraction, water chemistry, roast development, processing methods, and brew ratios.
body:
![A gooseneck kettle pouring water over a pour-over dripper](assets/images/pour-over.svg)

# The Nerdy Stuff

This page exists because people keep asking, and because I (Priya) genuinely cannot help myself. None of this is required reading to enjoy a coffee here — but if you've ever wondered why the same beans taste different depending on who makes them, this is why.

## Extraction, in One Paragraph

When hot water passes over ground coffee, it dissolves soluble compounds out of the grounds — acids, sugars, and various aromatic compounds, roughly in that order of solubility. **Extraction yield** is the percentage of the dry coffee's mass that ends up dissolved in your cup. Most agreed-upon "good" extraction sits between 18% and 22%. Below that, you're under-extracting: the drink tastes sour and thin because you've pulled out the acids but not enough of the sugars and body that balance them. Above that, you're over-extracting: you've pulled out bitter, papery compounds that only dissolve once the easier stuff is gone, and the cup tastes harsh and hollow.

**Total dissolved solids (TDS)** is the concentration of that dissolved coffee in the final drink — how strong it tastes, independent of how much was extracted from the grounds. You can hit a perfect 20% extraction yield and still make a cup that's too weak or too strong, because TDS also depends on your brew ratio. The two numbers together — extraction yield and TDS — are what a refractometer actually measures, and they're what separates "good coffee" from "good coffee, on purpose."

## Brew Ratios, Cheat Sheet

Ratio is grams of water to grams of dry coffee. These are our house starting points — adjust to taste, and if you want to nerd out with us, ask for a refractometer reading on your next cup.

| Method | Ratio (coffee:water) | Water Temp | Total Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Espresso | 1:2 | 93–96°C | 25–30 sec |
| V60 | 1:16 | 92–96°C | 2:30–3:00 |
| AeroPress | 1:15 | 85–90°C | 1:30–2:00 |
| Batch Brew | 1:17 | 92–94°C | 4:00–5:00 |
| Cold Brew | 1:8 (concentrate) | room temp | 16–18 hrs |

## Water Is Most of the Drink

Coffee is 98–99% water, so water chemistry matters more than most people assume. Two things matter most: **hardness** (dissolved calcium and magnesium) and **alkalinity** (buffering capacity, mostly from bicarbonate). Water that's too soft extracts poorly and tastes flat — there isn't enough mineral content to bind with and carry flavour compounds. Water that's too hard over-extracts and can taste chalky, and if it's high in bicarbonate specifically, it mutes acidity, flattening exactly the brightness a light-roast Ethiopian is supposed to have.

The SCA's target water standard sits around 150 ppm total dissolved solids, 50–175 ppm calcium hardness, and a pH near neutral. We filter and remineralise our water in-house to hit roughly that target, rather than using tap water or straight reverse osmosis — pure RO water with nothing added actually tastes worse than a well-balanced tap, because it has nothing in it to extract into.

## Roast Development, Briefly

Roasting is a controlled application of heat that drives off moisture, triggers the Maillard reaction and then caramelisation, and eventually breaks down the bean's cell structure enough to release CO₂ audibly — **first crack**, usually somewhere around 196°C bean temperature. Everything before first crack is moisture loss and browning; everything after it is "development," and how long you hold the roast in that window (development time, usually expressed as a percentage of total roast time) is one of the biggest levers on final flavour.

Short development after first crack keeps more of the bean's original acidity and origin character — this is roughly what "light roast" means, and it's why our single-origin filter coffees are almost always light-to-medium. Longer development trades that acidity for more roast-driven sweetness and body, and pushed far enough you get **second crack**, a much quieter, higher-pitched sound that signals the sugars are now caramelising hard and the origin character is being replaced by roast character. We roast our espresso blend to just past first crack for body and sweetness, and our filter offerings well before second crack, to let the farm show through.

## Processing Methods

How the fruit is removed from the coffee seed before drying changes the cup as much as the roast does:

- **Washed (wet process)** — the fruit skin and pulp are mechanically removed and the beans are fermented briefly in water to strip the remaining mucilage, then washed and dried. This gives the cleanest, most transparent cup — you taste the bean and terroir with the least interference. Most of our Kenyan and Rwandan lots are washed.
- **Natural (dry process)** — the whole cherry is dried intact, with the seed fermenting inside the fruit for one to four weeks. This produces heavier body and pronounced fruit-forward, sometimes wine-like or fermented notes. Several of our Eth

title: New on the Bar: Kenya, Nyeri, Washed
keywords: Kenya, Nyeri, single origin, washed process, filter coffee, tasting notes
description: Tasting notes and sourcing details for our new washed Kenyan single origin from Nyeri County.
author: Priya Sathe
body:
New on the filter bar this week: a washed coffee from Nyeri County, Kenya, grown at around 1,750 metres by smallholder farmers delivering cherry to the Gakuyuini factory.

**In the cup:** blackcurrant, a bright, almost tomato-like acidity, and a long, syrupy finish. This is about as close as coffee gets to tasting like a specific fruit rather than "fruity" in the abstract.

**Why it tastes like this:** two things are doing the work. First, the SL28 and SL34 varietals grown widely in Kenya are genetically predisposed to intense, wine-like acidity — they were selected decades ago partly for drought resistance, but they carry this flavour signature as a side effect. Second, the washed process here is unusually rigorous: double fermentation (a dry ferment followed by a washed ferment) strips the mucilage more completely than a single-stage wash, which tends to produce an even cleaner, more transparent cup.

**How we're brewing it:** V60, 1:16, water just off the boil at 94°C. This coffee has enough acidity that a slightly coarser grind and shorter contact time keeps it bright without tipping sour. We're roasting it light — well before first crack development gets going — specifically to preserve that blackcurrant note; a darker roast would trade it for generic roast sweetness.

Available by the cup at the bar, or as a 250g bag to take home. Ask for it by name — "the Kenyan" — and we'll know what you mean for the next few weeks, until it sells out.

title: Brewing Guide: V60, Our House Recipe
keywords: V60, pour over, brewing guide, recipe, coffee brewing
description: Our house V60 recipe and the reasoning behind each step.
author: Priya Sathe
body:
The V60 is the brew method we use most at the bar, and the one we get asked to explain most often. Here's our house recipe, plus the reasoning behind each step so you can adjust it instead of just copying it.

## The Recipe

- **Coffee:** 20g, medium-fine grind (think granulated sugar)
- **Water:** 320g, 94°C (about 30 seconds off a rolling boil at sea level)
- **Ratio:** 1:16
- **Total time:** 2:30–3:00

## Method

1. **Rinse the filter** with hot water, then discard the rinse water. This removes papery taste from the filter and preheats the dripper so it doesn't pull heat out of your brew.
2. **Add coffee, level the bed, and start your timer as you begin pouring.**
3. **Bloom:** pour 40g of water (2x the coffee weight) in a slow spiral, just enough to saturate all the grounds. Wait 30–45 seconds. This is the CO₂ escaping — you'll see it bubble and rise. Skipping the bloom means that gas escapes unevenly during the main pour instead, which pushes water away from parts of the coffee bed and causes uneven extraction.
4. **Main pour:** pour the remaining 280g in slow concentric circles, working from the centre outward and back, avoiding the very edge of the filter. Aim to finish adding water by around 1:45–2:00.
5. **Let it drain fully.** Total time from first pour to the last drip should land around 2:30–3:00. Faster than that and you're likely under-extracted (thin, sour); much slower and you're probably over-extracted (bitter, muddy) or your grind is too fine.

## Why These Numbers

A 1:16 ratio is a reasonable middle ground for filter coffee — strong enough to taste like something, dilute enough that a slight timing error doesn't ruin the cup. If you like a bolder cup, go to 1:15; for something lighter, 1:17. The bloom water at 2x coffee weight is enough to fully saturate the grounds without starting real extraction before the gas has a chance to escape.

Grind size is the lever to reach for if your timing is off: too fast (under 2:15) and the cup tastes sour or weak — grind finer. Too slow (over 3:15) and it tastes bitter or muddy — grind coarser. Water temperature matters too, but grind size is the bigger, easier-to-control variable, so change one thing at a time.

Come ask us at the bar if you want to see it done, or grab a bag and a V60 to try at home — we sell both.

title: New on the Bar: Ethiopia, Yirgacheffe, Natural
keywords: Ethiopia, Yirgacheffe, natural process, single origin, filter coffee, tasting notes
description: Tasting notes for our natural-processed Ethiopian single origin from Yirgacheffe.
author: Priya Sathe
body:
This week's filter bar coffee is a natural-processed lot from the Yirgacheffe growing region in southern Ethiopia, grown by smallholders at 1,900–2,100 metres and processed at a local washing station despite the name — "natural" here refers to the drying method, not the station.

**In the cup:** strawberry, jasmine, and a fermented, almost wine-like sweetness underneath. This is a much heavier-bodied, more intensely fruity cup than the washed Kenyan we ran in February, and it's a good side-by-side if you want to taste what processing method alone can do to the same broad region's coffee.

**Why it tastes like this:** in natural processing, the whole cherry is dried intact with the seed still inside the fruit, for two to four weeks depending on weather. The seed ferments surrounded by fruit sugars the entire time, which is where the strawberry and wine-like notes come from — they're fermentation byproducts that get absorbed into the bean, not something added afterward. It's a riskier method than washing (uneven drying can introduce off-flavours), which is part of why a clean natural lot commands a premium.

**How we're brewing it:** AeroPress, inverted, 1:15, 88°C, 2-minute steep. The heavier body and lower acidity of this lot holds up well to the fuller immersion brewing gives you, and the slightly lower temperature keeps the fermented notes from tipping into anything overripe.

By the cup or by the bag — ask for "the Ethiopian natural" at the counter.

title: The Water Chemistry Deep Dive We Promised
keywords: water chemistry, coffee science, hardness, alkalinity, TDS, SCA water standard
description: A deeper look at water chemistry and how hardness and alkalinity change extraction and flavour.
author: Priya Sathe
body:
I mentioned water chemistry on [the nerdy stuff](../the-nerdy-stuff.md) page in passing and got enough questions at the bar that it's earned its own post.

## Two Numbers That Matter Most

**General hardness (GH)** is the concentration of dissolved calcium and magnesium ions. These ions bind to flavour and aroma compounds during brewing and effectively carry them into solution — water with too little mineral content (like distilled or pure reverse-osmosis water) extracts poorly and produces a flat, one-dimensional cup no matter how carefully you brew, because there's nothing in the water to do that carrying.

**Alkalinity**, mostly driven by dissolved bicarbonate, is the water's buffering capacity — its ability to neutralise acid. This is the one that surprises people: high-alkalinity water actively fights against the acids in coffee, muting brightness and making everything taste flatter and duller. It's why the same beans can taste noticeably different brewed with tap water in two different cities — municipal water alkalinity varies hugely by region, and it has nothing to do with the coffee itself.

## The SCA Target

The Specialty Coffee Association publishes a target water standard: roughly 150 ppm total dissolved solids, calcium hardness between 50 and 175 ppm (as CaCO₃), alkalinity around 40 ppm, and a pH close to neutral (6.5–7.5). It's a range, not a single number, because different coffees and roast levels respond differently — a washed, high-acid coffee can handle (and benefits from) water toward the lower end of the hardness range, letting acidity shine, while a darker roast can take slightly higher mineral content without tasting harsh.

## What We Actually Do

Our municipal water here in Elmsworth runs moderately hard with fairly high alkalinity — fine for tea, rough on filter coffee, since the alkalinity flattens exactly the acidity we're trying to showcase in a light-roast Ethiopian or Kenyan. We run it through a carbon block filter to strip chlorine and particulate, then blend in a small amount of a mineral concentrate (mostly calcium and magnesium salts) to bring hardness back up to spec without the alkalinity that came with the original tap water. It's a small, unglamorous piece of equipment sitting under the counter, and it's arguably the single highest-leverage thing we've done for cup quality that has nothing to do with the coffee itself.

If you brew at home and have never tasted the same beans with filtered, remineralised water versus your tap, it's worth trying — for a lot of people it's a bigger difference than switching grinders.

title: Notes from a Sourcing Trip to Huehuetenango
keywords: sourcing trip, Guatemala, Huehuetenango, direct trade, roastery notes
description: Notes from a sourcing trip to Huehuetenango, Guatemala, visiting the farm we buy from.
author: Priya Sathe
body:
I spent the first week of October in Huehuetenango, in the western highlands of Guatemala, visiting the cooperative we've bought from for three harvests running. This is the fourth sourcing trip we've done since opening, and it's still the part of the job that reminds me why any of this is worth doing carefully.

The farms here sit between 1,500 and 2,000 metres, which is high enough that frost is an occasional real risk — something I hadn't fully appreciated until a farmer walked me through a stand of trees still showing damage from a cold snap two years back. High elevation is a big part of why this region's coffee has the density and structure it does: the plants grow more slowly at altitude, and slower growth means more time for sugars to develop in the cherry. But it's also a genuine agricultural risk that the farmers manage constantly, not just a marketing detail on a bag.

I spent a morning on the wet mill watching this year's harvest get depulped and moved into fermentation tanks, timed by taste and touch rather than a clock — the person running the mill has done this for over twenty years and can tell the mucilage is ready to wash off by feel, which is a skill I have enormous respect for and no ability to replicate myself. We cupped six lots together, in the same room, using the same protocol we use back home, and picked the two we're bringing back this year based on that session rather than on samples that arrived by mail months ago.

We pay above the cooperative's standard export price, on a contract we agree before the harvest so the farmers know what they're growing for rather than finding out at sale time. It's a small operation on our end — we're buying maybe 2,000kg a year from this cooperative, which is nothing compared to what larger roasters move — but the relationship is real, and I'd rather have four farms I actually visit than forty I only know from a spec sheet.

New lot from this trip lands on the bar in a few weeks, once it's shipped, rested, and roasted. I'll post tasting notes when it's ready.

title: Brewing Guide: AeroPress, Inverted Method
keywords: AeroPress, brewing guide, recipe, inverted method, coffee brewing
description: Our house AeroPress recipe using the inverted method, and why we brew it this way.
author: Priya Sathe
body:
The AeroPress is the brew method we recommend most for travel and home use — cheap, close to indestructible, and forgiving of a slightly wrong grind in a way a V60 isn't. Here's our house recipe.

## The Recipe

- **Coffee:** 16g, medium grind (slightly coarser than table salt)
- **Water:** 240g, 88°C
- **Ratio:** 1:15
- **Total time:** ~2:00

## Method

1. **Invert the AeroPress** — plunger inserted a short way into the chamber, resting upside down on the wide end. This lets you do a full immersion steep before pressing, rather than water dripping through immediately like the standard method.
2. **Add coffee, then water**, all 240g at once, and stir gently for 10 seconds to make sure all the grounds are saturated.
3. **Steep for 1:30.** This is a full immersion brew for most of that time, which is why the grind can be a bit coarser and more forgiving than a pour-over — the coffee has much longer contact with the water regardless of flow rate.
4. **Attach the rinsed filter and cap**, carefully flip the whole assembly onto your cup, and press slowly and steadily over about 20–30 seconds. You want gentle, even resistance — if it's very hard to press, your grind is too fine; if it slides through with no resistance at all, too coarse.

## Why the Inverted Method

Standard (right-side-up) AeroPress use starts extracting the moment you add water, since it's already sitting on the filter and gravity pulls water through immediately — hard to control precisely, and prone to dripping through before you're ready to press. Inverting turns the AeroPress into a sealed immersion brewer for the steep phase, giving you full control over contact time independent of press speed. It's a small change that makes the method noticeably more consistent.

Lower water temperature than a V60 (88°C vs. 94°C) balances out the longer contact time — full immersion for 90 seconds at 94°C would push a lot of coffees into over-extraction. If you're brewing a very light roast and want more clarity, bump the temperature up to 90–92°C and shorten the steep slightly.

We keep three AeroPresses behind the counter for our own use on slow mornings — it's genuinely a great everyday brewer, not just a travel backup.

title: Light, Medium, Dark: What Roast Levels Actually Mean
keywords: roast levels, light roast, dark roast, coffee science, roast curve
description: What light, medium, and dark roast levels actually mean, and why we roast almost everything on the lighter end.
author: Priya Sathe
body:
"Light roast" and "dark roast" get used as flavour descriptors — light means bright and acidic, dark means bold and smoky — but they're really describing a point on a temperature and time curve, and the flavour follows from the chemistry, not the label itself.

## What's Actually Changing

As a roast progresses, three things happen roughly in sequence: **moisture evaporates**, the bean undergoes the **Maillard reaction** (the same browning reaction that happens searing a steak or baking bread, producing hundreds of new aromatic compounds), and then **caramelisation** kicks in as sugars break down under heat. Sitting on top of all this, the bean's cell walls are drying out and becoming brittle, until they crack audibly — first crack, then, if you keep going, second crack.

- **Light roast** stops shortly after first crack. Origin character — the acidity, florals, and fruit notes that come from the variety and terroir — is at its most preserved, because there's been the least time for roast-driven flavours to build up and mask it. This is almost everything we run on the filter bar.
- **Medium roast** extends further past first crack, letting caramelisation develop more body and sweetness while still keeping some origin character. A reasonable middle ground for people who find light roasts too sharp.
- **Dark roast** pushes toward or past second crack. By this point, the bean's own oils are being forced to the surface, roast-driven bitterness and smokiness dominate, and most of the acidity and origin nuance is gone — replaced by flavours that come from the roasting process itself rather than the farm. This isn't a flaw; it's just a different, roast-forward style, and it's why a dark-roast espresso and a light-roast Ethiopian can taste like they came from different beverages entirely.

## Why We Lean Light

Origin coffee is expensive to source well, and a large part of what you're paying for is the specific character of that farm, that varietal, that processing method, in that year's harvest. Roasting dark tends to burn that specificity away and replace it with a flavour profile — bittersweet, smoky, heavy — that's fairly similar across different origins. We'd rather let you taste the difference between the Kenyan and the Guatemalan than roast them both to a point where they converge.

That said, our espresso blend is roasted a bit further than our filter offerings — just past first crack, with more development — because body and sweetness matter more in an espresso shot cut with milk, and because a very light roast can taste sour and thin under high-pressure extraction if it hasn't developed enough. Right roast for the right brew method, not one philosophy applied everywhere.

title: The Physics of Steamed Milk
keywords: milk steaming, microfoam, latte, coffee science, steam wand
description: The science of steaming milk for espresso drinks — microfoam, protein structure, and why timing matters.
author: Marcus Oduya
body:
I'm Marcus, one of the baristas here, and after four years behind the machine I've thought about steamed milk more than any reasonable person should. Here's what's actually happening when you steam.

## What Microfoam Is

Good microfoam is milk with tiny, evenly distributed air bubbles — small enough that the texture reads as silky rather than foamy, and the milk pours as a cohesive liquid rather than separating into foam and liquid layers. It's not about how much air you add; it's about how finely and evenly it's distributed. Overly large bubbles collapse quickly and separate, which is why a bad cappuccino has a dry, clumpy foam cap that looks nothing like the milk underneath it.

## The Two Phases

**Stretching:** the steam wand tip sits just below the milk's surface, pulling in air and creating that fine bubble structure. This should happen early and briefly — a few seconds, judged by a distinct "tearing paper" sound rather than a hiss or a slurp. Stretch too long and the bubbles get large and unstable; stretch too little and you get flat, dense milk with no texture at all.

**Texturing:** the wand tip is submerged deeper, creating a whirlpool that spins the milk and breaks up any remaining large bubbles into the fine, even microfoam you want, while also distributing heat evenly. This phase does the actual polishing of the texture.

## Why Temperature Matters

Milk proteins (mainly casein and whey) start to denature — unfold and change structure — around 65–70°C, which is part of what gives steamed milk its sweeter taste compared to cold milk: heat breaks down lactose slightly and makes it taste more perceptibly sweet. But push past about 70°C and you start to scald the milk, breaking down proteins further in a way that produces a slightly cooked, less pleasant flavour and can collapse the foam structure you just built. We steam to 60–65°C and stop — check the pitcher temperature by hand against the outside, not by sound alone, since sound is a much less reliable signal once you're already past the ideal window.

## Why Oat Milk Behaves Differently

Oat milk foams differently from dairy because it has no casein — it relies on added stabilisers (usually gums or emulsifiers) and its own starches to hold air, rather than milk proteins. It tends to foam faster and can go from good texture to over-stretched more quickly than dairy, so we generally cut the stretching phase shorter for oat milk drinks. Almond and soy milk each behave slightly differently again — if your favourite alt-milk latte tastes different at another café, milk choice and steaming technique are both doing a lot of that work, not just the espresso.

Come watch the bar on a slow morning — I'm always happy to talk through it while I pull a shot.

title: A Rare One: Panama Geisha, Washed
keywords: Panama Geisha, single origin, washed process, rare coffee, tasting notes
description: Tasting notes and pricing for a limited-lot washed Geisha from Panama.
author: Priya Sathe
body:
We don't run this coffee often, because we can't get much of it and it isn't cheap, but a small lot of washed Geisha from a high-altitude farm in the Panama highlands just arrived, and it's worth talking about even if most of it will sell out within the week.

**In the cup:** jasmine, bergamot, and a delicate, tea-like sweetness, with a lightness of body that reads almost more like a fine tea than a coffee. This is the coffee that made Geisha famous when a Panamanian lot took the coffee world by surprise at auction in 2004, and two decades on, well-grown Geisha still tastes like nothing else we serve.

**Why it's different:** Geisha (sometimes spelled Gesha) is a distinct varietal, originally from Ethiopia, that happened to thrive unusually well when grown at high altitude in a handful of Central American microclimates. It's a genuinely different genetic line from the Bourbon and Typica varietals underlying most of what we sell, and it produces a floral, tea-like cup profile almost regardless of how it's processed — though washed processing, like this lot, tends to show that floral character most clearly, with the least interference.

**Why it's expensive:** the plants are lower-yielding than more common varietals, the best lots come from a small number of specific microclimates, and demand from roasters chasing that jasmine-bergamot profile has pushed prices at auction into genuinely extraordinary territory for the very top lots. What we have isn't an auction-lot rarity, but it's still a small, carefully selected batch, and it's priced accordingly — $9 for a cup, $34 for a 100g bag (yes, 100g, not 250g).

**How we're brewing it:** V60, 1:17 — slightly more dilute than our usual filter ratio, since this coffee's delicate florals get lost if the cup is too concentrated. Water at 92°C, a touch cooler than usual, to keep the jasmine notes from tipping into anything sharp.

Limited quantity, first-come. Worth it, at least once.

title: Brewing Guide: Cold Brew, Our House Method
keywords: cold brew, brewing guide, recipe, coffee brewing
description: Our house cold brew recipe, how it differs from iced hot-brewed coffee, and why the ratio is so different.
author: Marcus Oduya
body:
People sometimes assume cold brew is just iced coffee, but it's a genuinely different extraction process, and it's worth understanding why the recipe looks so different from anything you'd use with hot water.

## The Recipe

- **Coffee:** coarse grind (coarser than you'd use for a French press), 1:8 ratio with room-temperature or cold filtered water
- **Steep:** 16–18 hours at room temperature, or slightly longer in the fridge
- **Filter:** through a paper filter or fine mesh, twice if the first pass leaves sediment
- **Serve:** the result is a concentrate — dilute roughly 1:1 with water or milk over ice to taste

## Why It's So Different From Hot Brewing

Extraction happens faster at higher temperatures because heat speeds up the rate at which soluble compounds dissolve out of the coffee grounds — the same reason tea steeps faster in boiling water than in cold water. Cold brew compensates for the much slower extraction rate by trading time for temperature: instead of 2–5 minutes at 90+°C, you get 16+ hours at room temperature or below.

That long, cold steep doesn't just extract more slowly — it extracts *differently*. Certain acids and aromatic compounds are more soluble at higher temperatures than others, so a cold, slow extraction pulls a different ratio of compounds out of the same beans compared to a hot brew, even accounting for time. Cold brew consistently comes out lower in perceived acidity and higher in body and sweetness than the same beans brewed hot, which is why it's often described as "smoother" — it's not smoother because it's less strong (it's usually stronger, hence diluting it), it's smoother because the chemistry of what's dissolved is genuinely different.

## Why We Use a Concentrate, Not a Ready-to-Drink Ratio

Brewing at 1:8 and diluting to taste at serving time, rather than brewing straight to drinking strength, keeps the concentrate stable and useful for longer (it keeps about two weeks refrigerated), lets us serve it over ice without over-diluting from the ice melt, and gives us — and you — control over strength per drink rather than one fixed recipe for everyone.

We batch-brew this in a large cold brew tower behind the counter, started the evening before service, so it's ready fresh for us each morning rather than sitting around for days on end.

title: Latte Art Basics: Why It's Harder Than It Looks
keywords: latte art, espresso, microfoam, pouring technique
description: Why latte art is genuinely difficult, and the basics of pouring a simple heart and rosetta.
author: Marcus Oduya
body:
People often assume latte art is decorative and separate from making a good drink. It's actually a fairly direct readout of whether the milk and espresso were both done right — you cannot fake good latte art with bad microfoam or a bad shot, which is part of why we take it seriously rather than treating it as a party trick.

## What Has to Go Right Before You Even Start Pouring

The espresso needs a good layer of crema, and the milk needs properly textured microfoam — fine, even bubbles, poured while still genuinely liquid rather than stiff and foam-like. If either of those is off, no pouring technique will produce a clean pattern; the contrast between the white microfoam and the brown crema is what actually draws the picture, and if the milk's too airy or the crema's broken up, there's nothing for the pattern to show up against.

## The Basic Heart

1. Pour steadily from a height of a few centimetres into the centre of the cup, tilted at roughly a 45-degree angle, letting the cup fill most of the way with espresso and milk mixing underneath the surface.
2. Once the cup is nearly full, lower the pitcher spout close to the surface and pour a steady, focused stream directly into the centre — this is where the white circle starts to appear on the surface.
3. As the circle grows to fill most of the cup, pull the pitcher back toward the rim while gently swaying it in a straight line, then lift and cut through the middle at the end — that final motion draws the point of the heart.

## The Rosetta

Same setup, but instead of holding the pour still, you wiggle the pitcher gently side to side while slowly pulling backward across the cup, which lays down a series of connected leaf-like shapes. It's a more advanced pour because the wiggle has to stay consistent in both amplitude and timing while your hand is also moving backward — most people find their wiggle drifts as they focus on the pullback, and vice versa.

## Why It Takes Longer to Learn Than People Expect

The hard part isn't the wrist motion — it's building a feel for micro-adjustments in pour height, angle, and speed that respond to how a specific pitcher, cup shape, and milk texture behave together, and that feel doesn't transfer directly between different equipment. Most of our baristas take a few months of regular practice before their hearts are consistently clean, and rosettas take longer still. If yours doesn't look like ours on the first try at home, that's completely normal — it took us a while too.

title: New on the Bar: Guatemala, Huehuetenango, Honey Process
keywords: Guatemala, Huehuetenango, honey process, single origin, filter coffee, tasting notes
description: Tasting notes for our honey-processed Guatemalan single origin from the Huehuetenango cooperative we visited in 2024.
author: Priya Sathe
body:
This is the lot from the cooperative in Huehuetenango I visited back in October 2024 — it's taken until now to ship, rest, and get roasted, and it was worth the wait. This year they processed part of the harvest as red honey rather than fully washed, and we picked it specifically to run alongside our usual washed offering from the same farm.

**In the cup:** dried apricot, brown sugar, and a rounder, fuller body than the washed lot from this same cooperative, with noticeably less sharp acidity.

**Why it tastes like this:** in honey processing, the skin is removed but some of the sticky mucilage layer is left on the parchment during drying — "red honey" means a moderate amount of mucilage retained, more than yellow honey, less than black. That retained mucilage keeps fermenting gently during the drying period, adding body and a stone-fruit sweetness that a fully washed process (where the mucilage is stripped off before drying) doesn't develop. It's genuinely a middle ground between the clarity of washed coffee and the intensity of a full natural.

**Side by side with the washed lot:** if you want to actually taste what processing does independent of terroir, ask for the cupping flight this week — we're running this honey lot next to the cooperative's washed lot from the same farm, same harvest. Same trees, same altitude, same varietal, genuinely different cup.

**How we're brewing it:** batch brew, 1:17, 93°C. The fuller body carries well through batch brewing, and this is a good "house coffee" cup for anyone who finds our usual washed African lots too sharp.

On the bar now, while it lasts — this is a smaller lot than usual, since the cooperative only honey-processed a fraction of this harvest as an experiment.

title: How to Read a Roast Curve
keywords: roast curve, roast log, coffee science, first crack, development time, RoR
description: How to read a roast curve — bean temperature, rate of rise, and development time.
author: Priya Sathe
body:
A few regulars have asked what the printouts taped up by the roaster actually mean, so here's how to read one.

## The Two Lines

A roast curve plots two things against time: **bean temperature** (BT), the actual temperature of the coffee itself, and **rate of rise** (RoR), how fast that temperature is climbing at any given moment. BT tells you where you are in the roast; RoR tells you how quickly you're getting there, which matters just as much — the same end temperature reached quickly versus slowly produces a different-tasting bean, because it changes how much time the Maillard reaction and caramelisation get to develop relative to how fast moisture and structure are changing.

## Reading the Shape

A healthy roast curve shows RoR declining smoothly through the roast — climbing fast early (drying out the bean), then gradually slowing as the roast progresses. What you want to avoid is a "flat spot" or, worse, an RoR that flatlines or ticks upward late in the roast: that usually means heat input hasn't been reduced enough as the bean's own exothermic reactions start contributing heat on top of the roaster's applied heat, which risks a scorched, harsh-tasting result even if the final temperature looks correct on paper. A sharp early spike followed by too rapid a decline, on the other hand, tends to produce an underdeveloped, grassy, "baked" cup — the bean hit temperature too fast without proper development.

## Marking First Crack

First crack shows up on the curve as a distinct point, usually around 196°C BT, and a good roast log marks the exact time and temperature it starts and how long it lasts. Everything from that point to the end of the roast is "development time" — we track it as a percentage of total roast time (development time ratio, or DTR). For our filter coffees we're usually targeting 15–18% DTR; for the espresso blend, closer to 20–22%, since that drink needs the extra body and sweetness that comes with more time past first crack.

## Why We Keep and Post These

Every roast gets logged — batch size, charge temperature, first crack time and temperature, DTR, and total roast time — and we keep them because a curve that looks right on paper doesn't always mean the cup was right, and a curve with a small deviation doesn't always mean the cup was wrong. Comparing curves against cupping notes over dozens of roasts of the same lot is how we actually dial in a profile, rather than getting it right once and hoping it repeats.

If you're roasting at home on a small sample roaster, the single biggest upgrade you can make isn't a fancier machine — it's logging your roasts against a curve and your own tasting notes, consistently, so you can actually see what a change did instead of guessing.
